title: UOB shifts AI focus from adoption to returns
excerpt: 1 day ago. UOB shifts AI focus from adoption to returns. The bank targets 900 million in projected AI value by 2030. United Overseas Bank (UOB) is shifting its artificial intelligence (AI) strategy towards measurable financial returns, targeting 900 million in projected economic value by 2030 as it moves beyond broad workforce adoption. Lee Zhu Kuang, managing director and group head of Innovation Group at UOB, said widespread AI use builds workforce capabilities, but targeted automation delivers the business impact. Join Singapore Business Review community. With more than 30,000 employees using Copilot daily and 90% upskilled in generative AI, UOB is measuring returns through revenue growth, productivity improvements and risk reduction rather than adoption rates alone. "Adoption is not ROI itself," Lee said, stressing that specific AI initiatives must generate tangible economic value. The distinction is becoming increasingly important as banks transition from generative AI tools towards agentic systems capable of executing tasks across business operations. Lee expects these systems to reduce processing times, eliminate operational friction and improve cost efficiency. However, greater autonomy also introduces governance challenges. He said banks must establish clear boundaries around which decisions AI can recommend, execute independently or escalate for human approval. AI decisions must also remain traceable, explainable and auditable. "Human accountability, especially on material decisions, should not be delegated to AI," Lee said. The bank is also adjusting its approach to workforce development as automation takes over repetitive analytical tasks traditionally handled by junior employees. Lee said AI could help younger employees develop judgment, creativity and business understanding earlier in their careers rather than spend time on routine work. Looking towards 2027, he expects AI to evolve from a standalone productivity tool into technology that coordinates workflows across banking operations. Beyond cost reductions, Lee identified more responsive, personalised and resilient banking services as potential sources of competitive advantage. "Success will not be determined by who deploys the most AI, but it will be determined by who can actually scale trusted AI better," he said.

title: Better Markets Slams OCC's AI Lending Framework
excerpt: . Better Markets Slams OCC's AI Lending Framework. The nonprofit says the agency's new artificial intelligence guidance for banks leaves loan applicants unprotected from unexplained AI credit rejections. Updated on Nov. 25, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence. Live Poll. Do you trust banks to use AI fairly when deciding your loan applications?. Better Markets, a nonprofit economic advocacy organization, released a fact sheet criticizing the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's artificial intelligence supervisory framework for banks. The group argues the framework does not address the risk that AI models can reject creditworthy applicants without a clear reason. Why it matters. The OCC charters and supervises national banks, so its guidance shapes how lenders use AI in credit decisions nationwide. Critics say leaving fair-lending responsibility to individual banks could leave consumers with no clear explanation when an AI model denies them a loan. The critique rests on the framework's omissions rather than on measured lending outcomes, and the three federal banking agencies named (OCC, Federal Reserve, FDIC) are the bodies whose AI oversight is being compared. No loan denial rates or audit findings were included in the report, leaving the scale of the alleged risk unquantified. The players. Better Markets. Better Markets is a nonprofit economic advocacy organization that focuses on financial reform and regulatory oversight of banks and markets. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency is the federal agency that charters, regulates and supervises national banks in the United States. The details. Better Markets said the OCC framework is inconsistent on whether AI counts as a separate risk category and does not state that bank boards and senior managers are ultimately responsible for AI risks. The group's report last week called for a guaranteed explanation for every adverse AI credit decision and independent audits of lending models. Timeline. Monday, November 23, 2026: Better Markets released its fact sheet criticizing the OCC framework. Last week, before November 23, 2026: Better Markets released its broader report calling for AI credit-denial explanations and model audits. Related coverage. Banking. Nov. 10. Banks Tighten Controls on AI Agents Amid Rogue Risks. Roadmap. The OCC's new AI guidance for banks is the agency's framework for overseeing how lenders deploy artificial intelligence in their operations. Better Markets' critique places this federal supervisory approach against calls for explicit explanation rights and independent model audits in consumer lending. If you apply for a bank loan, an AI model may influence the decision, and under the current framework you may not receive a specific reason for a denial. Ask your lender whether automated tools were used in your application and request the principal reasons for any adverse decision. The takeaway. Automated lending decisions can affect your access to credit even when no person reviewed your file. Knowing that regulators have left the explanation requirement open gives you a reason to ask lenders directly how their AI decisions are made. Further reading. title: Agentic AI adoption by global banks could put further pressure on Indian IT revenues
excerpt: Artificial Intelligence. 1 min read. Agentic AI adoption by global banks could put further pressure on Indian IT revenues. Agentic AI adoption across global banking firms is rapidly improving productivity and reducing operational costs, as noted in a recent report. Indian IT services companies face declining revenues from traditional sources due to these advancements, creating a challenging environment. While AI is still in the early stages, significant growth opportunities exist for mid-tier IT firms. Select financial services firms report productivity gains of 20-40 percent from AI-driven efficiencies. ANI. Published On Nov 26, 2026 at 03:00 PM IST. Set ETCIO as your preferred source on Google. The increasing adoption of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) by global banking and financial services firms could put further pressure on traditional revenues of Indian IT services companies, even as rising AI investments create strong growth opportunities for mid-tier IT firms, according to a report by Kotak Institutional Equities. The report noted that technology spending by US and European banks remains healthy, with AI adoption expanding rapidly across business operations, improving productivity and helping firms achieve cost-saving targets. Banks are also gradually adopting AI agents and agentic AI to further enhance operational efficiency. Advt. Despite this progress, AI adoption remains at an early stage, offering significant growth opportunities for Indian IT services firms. Aggregate revenues of Indian IT services firms from the banking, financial services and insurance (BFSI) segment grew at a moderate 6. 1 per cent year-on-year in the September 2026 quarter. "Incumbents are at the risk of further deflation in the base business from an increase in productivity benefits in software development due to agentic AI adoption," the report said. Select global financial services firms have reported productivity gains of 20-40 per cent in software development through AI adoption. However, these gains could increase further as developers increasingly adopt autonomous coding tools and AI agents. The report further highlighted that AI-driven efficiencies could reduce incremental workforce requirements across financial services firms, particularly in customer service and Know Your Customer (KYC) operations. "AI efficiencies are expected to reduce incremental headcount needs for growth and backfilling attrition," it said. In technology functions, however, the focus remains largely on limiting fresh hiring and utilising excess capacity to accelerate product development and innovation. Overall, "Incumbents are at the risk of further deflation in the base business from an increase in productivity benefits in software development due to agentic AI adoption," it said. ANI. title: Are US banks warning customers they could be responsible for AI agents' errors?
excerpt: Claim: In November, U. S. banks warned customers they could be liable for money lost to mistakes made by artificial intelligence agents acting on their behalf. Rating:. title: Tech Firms Launch AI Assistants as Banks Block Agents
excerpt: . Tech Firms Launch AI Assistants as Banks Block Agents. Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic launched AI personal assistants Muse, dots and Claude Duet within weeks of each other. Royal Bank, TD Bank, CIBC and Bank of Montreal blocked third-party AI agents from directly accessing clients' online bank accounts. Why it matters. The launches show AI agents moving from answering questions to taking actions such as sending emails and making purchases on users' behalf. The bank restrictions reflect concern that handing these tools sensitive financial information carries real risk. OpenAI's dots can be connected to more than 4,000 apps and other devices, while Muse runs on its own dedicated cloud computer and checks with users before sensitive actions. Muse can send emails, book travel and make purchases when linked to apps such as Shopify and Ticketmaster, and it keeps working on multiple tasks while the app is closed. Muse is free, while dots and Claude Duet require a subscription, and Claude Duet is not available in Canada. title: Moon Tae-yoon Wins World Bank AI Agriculture Hackathon
excerpt: . Moon Tae-yoon Wins World Bank AI Agriculture Hackathon. A University of Seoul student's Dure system uses text messages from basic phones to coordinate collective shipment of farm produce. Updated on Nov. 20, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence. Moon Tae-yoon won first place in the agriculture track of the Small AI for Development Hackathon Challenge hosted by the World Bank Group, held October 3-4. He competed as an individual and was later invited to present his Dure solution at the Global AI & Digital Summit 2026 in Seoul. Why it matters. Smallholder farmers often struggle to negotiate fair prices when selling alone, while formal cooperatives require administrative procedures, initial capital and consensus that can be hard to reach. Dure offers a lower-barrier alternative that works over basic mobile phones, with potential relevance for agricultural markets in developing countries. Dure was judged first among agriculture-track entries at a two-day World Bank Group hackathon, ahead of teams from UC Berkeley and Carnegie Mellon University. Whether the system has been tested with real farming groups in the field is not reported. The players. World Bank Group. The World Bank Group is an international financial institution that provides loans and technical assistance to developing countries, and it hosted the Small AI for Development Hackathon Challenge. Moon Tae-yoon. Moon Tae-yoon is a University of Seoul student who won the agriculture track and developed the Dure system. The details. Dure processes text messages in Tetum, one of Timor-Leste's official languages, and combines an ultralightweight language model with a rule-based engine. Moon Tae-yoon conceptualized and developed the system, and operated an exhibition booth demonstrating it at the summit, where he also presented the technical architecture in an official session. Timeline. October 3-4: Small AI for Development Hackathon Challenge held, where Moon won first place in the agriculture track. Its feature-phone, text-message design places it within that same push to bring AI tools to smallholder markets in developing countries. For smallholder farmers, a text-message tool could make it possible to join collective shipments without a formal cooperative, potentially improving prices for produce. Whether Dure is available to farmers outside the competition and summit settings has not been reported. The takeaway. title: KI im Asset Management: Zwischen Anspruch und Rendite
excerpt: Künstliche Intelligenz steht bei Asset Managern weit oben auf der Agenda. Doch wie wird aus einem vielversprechenden Pilotprojekt ein wirtschaftlich tragfähiger Prozess? Eine aktuelle Studie untersucht den Stand der Umsetzung und die Erfolgsfaktoren. KI verstehen. Künstliche Intelligenz verändert die Arbeitsabläufe und Geschäftsmodelle im Asset Management. Neben der Unterstützung von Anlageentscheidungen bieten sich Einsatzmöglichkeiten in der Fondsadministration, im Risikomanagement und bei der Verarbeitung großer Datenmengen. Für Kapitalverwaltungsgesellschaften, Verwahrstellen und Banken mit eigenem Asset Management stellt sich dabei zunehmend die Frage, wie sich einzelne Anwendungen in bestehende Prozesse integrieren und wirtschaftlich betreiben lassen. Partner des Bank Blogs. Eine aktuelle Studie von KPMG untersucht, wie weit die Branche bei der Einführung und Skalierung künstlicher Intelligenz vorangekommen ist. Grundlage sind Experteninterviews mit Verantwortlichen aus dem COO-Ressort von Asset Managern, Servicing-Anbietern und Verwahrstellen. Aus den Interviews wurden mehr als 640 Einzelbewertungen ausgewertet. KI verstehen. KI besitzt hohe strategische Bedeutung. Die Bedeutung künstlicher Intelligenz für das Asset Management wird von den befragten Unternehmen einhellig anerkannt. Sämtliche Teilnehmer stufen die Technologie als strategisch wichtig ein. Für 75 Prozent ist sie sogar kritisch oder existenzentscheidend für die eigene Wettbewerbsfähigkeit. Damit hat KI in der Branche einen hohen Stellenwert erreicht. Sie wird nicht mehr ausschließlich als Instrument zur Automatisierung einzelner Tätigkeiten betrachtet, sondern als Technologie, die langfristig Einfluss auf Kostenstrukturen, Leistungsfähigkeit und Geschäftsmodelle nehmen kann. Die hohe strategische Bedeutung bedeutet allerdings nicht, dass die Unternehmen bei der praktischen Umsetzung bereits entsprechend weit vorangekommen sind. excerpt: A third (33%) of UK adults say they have seen an investment promotion in the past year that they believe used artificial intelligence (AI), new research from the FCA shows. Reports of investment fraud to Report Fraud that mention suspected use of AI have risen by nearly 400% in a year, up from 193 in 2024/25 to 956 in 2025/26. Investment fraud victims lost an average of £28,188 in 2025/26. Most people feel confident they could spot an AI investment scam, but that confidence is lower when a well-known person is involved. Almost two-thirds (62%) of adults say they could identify an investment scam that used AI. But less than half (49%) think they could tell whether a video or voice recording of a well-known person had been generated or altered by AI. Martin Lewis was the person most often named by those who thought they had seen a fake promotion featuring a well-known person. Under-35s are the most confident and the most exposed. Around three-quarters (74%) say they could identify an AI investment scam, and more than half (56%) believe they have seen an AI-generated investment promotion in the past year. Despite this, fewer than 4 in 10 (38%) would check whether a firm is FCA-authorised before investing. Among over-65s the figure is almost three-quarters (73%). Sheree Howard, executive director of authorisations at the FCA, said:. 'AI makes creating online scams easier and harder for people to identify. 'Whether you’re considering an investment, pension opportunity, loan or other financial service, use Firm Checker to check if a firm is authorised and help fight financial crime. '. Before you invest, check the firm. Search the FCA Firm Checker to see whether the firm is authorised for the services being offered. Use the firm contact details on Firm Checker to ensure you are dealing with the real firm. Firm Checker also lists firms the FCA knows are operating without authorisation. Notes to editors:. The survey was conducted by Kantar. The survey was conducted from 20 to 26 October 2026. The sample comprised 2,558 UK respondents aged 16+. References to investment promotions using AI mean AI-generated or manipulated media, such as video or audio. The investment fraud figures are taken from Report Fraud’s Annual Assessment FY2025-26 (PDF) , published in September 2026. Firm Checker has been specially designed for, and tested with, consumers to make sure it is effective and easy to use. The Financial Services Register remains in place as the full regulatory record of the authorised financial services population. Using an authorised firm can also bring other benefits as authorised firms must meet FCA standards and follow the FCA's rules. Consumers can also take a complaint to the Financial Ombudsman Service and are more likely to benefit from protection from the Financial Services Compensation Scheme. We strengthened consumer protection through the promotion of our Firm Checker tool. We estimate that the tool has been used over 1. 9 million times since its introduction in January 2025. Following an advertising campaign in January 2026, we saw a 49% increase in estimated consumers protected (from about 464 to 694 per week).
